God's verdict overturns the verdicts of the experts
The temple's cornerstone had a miraculous hidden origin
comprehension_check.why: Psalm 118:23 names the reversal as the LORD's own doing, his choice standing over the builders' rejection.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Psalm 118:22-23 again. Notice who did the rejecting, and who is named as the one behind the reversal.

nodes.title: Psalm 119: The Torah Psalm
nodes.summary: The Bible's longest chapter: a 176-verse acrostic love poem to God's word, eight lines for every letter of the Hebrew alphabet — 'Your word is a lamp to my feet,' 'I have hidden your word in my heart.' Devotion to Scripture rendered as art.

prerequisites.reason: The psalm is the Shema's 'these words on your heart' lived out at full length.

nodes.discussion_prompt: The writer of Psalm 119 spent 176 verses telling God how much he loves his word, crafting eight lines for every Hebrew letter. What would it take for Scripture to become something you delight in rather than something you feel guilty about skipping, and where would you start?
assessment_questions: What is unusual about Psalm 119's structure, and what single subject does nearly every verse touch?
The psalmist says it was good for him to be afflicted because affliction taught him God's statutes. What is he claiming about the relationship between hardship and God's word?
Psalm 119:11 speaks of hiding God's word in the heart as a defense against sin. What one verse would you actually memorize this week, and for what fight?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The psalm treats God's word as trustworthy light for every step, a lamp for the feet and a light on the path.
The psalmist loves, sings, and treasures the word, showing that Scripture is meant to shape desire and joy.
Affliction drives the psalmist deeper into God's promises, where he finds comfort and the strength to persevere.

teaching_concepts.concept: Meditation as a way of life
teaching_concepts.explanation: The psalm models slow, repeated reflection on Scripture as the path to wisdom, peace, and moral clarity.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe Psalm 119's acrostic design and explain, using two of its verses, what the psalmist believes God's word does for a person.

comprehension_check.question: Psalm 119 spends 176 verses praying about God's word. What does the psalm expect the word to do in a life?
options: Supply winning arguments for defeating opponents
Reward diligent study with prosperity and ease
Ward off harm whenever its lines are recited
Retrain the heart's desires and guide its steps
comprehension_check.why: Psalm 119:11 stores the word in the heart to keep from sin, and Psalm 119:105 has it lighting the path one step at a time.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Psalm 119:9-11 and Psalm 119:105 again. Notice where the word is kept, and what it is kept there for.

comprehension_check.question: Psalm 119 keeps mentioning affliction inside its love poem to the word. What does it teach prayer to do under trial?
options: Set Scripture aside until conditions allow study again
Press deeper into the promises while the trial lasts
Treat the pain as noise a mature believer ignores
Suspend obedience until God grants some visible relief
comprehension_check.why: Psalm 119:71 can call the affliction good because it taught the psalmist God's statutes, trouble driving him further into the word.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Psalm 119:67-71 again. Notice what the psalmist says the hard season actually did for him.

nodes.title: The Psalms of Ascent
nodes.summary: Fifteen short pilgrim songs sung on the climb up to Jerusalem's feasts: 'I lift my eyes to the hills' (121), 'I was glad when they said, let us go to the house of the LORD' (122), 'out of the depths I cry' (130). A pocket-sized psalter of trust for people on the road.

prerequisites.reason: The songs climb toward Zion — the city and sanctuary David established.

nodes.discussion_prompt: These fifteen songs were prayed on the road, in transit between home and the house of God. What journey or transition are you in right now, and which line from these psalms would you want in your pocket for it?
assessment_questions: What shared title do Psalms 120 through 134 carry, and what destination do they climb toward?
Psalm 121 promises the LORD will keep the traveler, yet pilgrims still faced heat, danger, and hard roads. What kind of keeping is the psalm actually promising?
Psalm 131 describes a soul calmed and quieted like a weaned child with its mother. What would you have to stop striving for to reach that kind of calm, and what is one step toward it?

teaching_concepts.explanation: These songs treat life with God as a journey toward his presence, prayed while still in motion.
Psalm 121 anchors the traveler's safety in God's unsleeping watch over every going out and coming in.
Psalm 130 shows the pilgrim crying from the bottom, trusting that forgiveness is with the LORD and waiting for him like a watchman for morning.
Psalm 122's gladness at going to the house of the LORD makes worship communal, tying personal faith to the peace of the whole city.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what the Psalms of Ascent were for, and walk through one of them showing how it turns a traveler's fear into trust.

comprehension_check.question: Psalm 121 answers its question about help by calling the LORD the pilgrim's keeper. What is the song teaching travelers to do?
options: Post their own watches so danger never finds them sleeping
Earn safe passage by completing the pilgrimage without complaint
Rest their safety on a watch that never sleeps
Read the hills themselves as shelter sent for them
comprehension_check.why: Psalm 121:3-4 gives the road to a keeper who never slumbers, and Psalm 121:8 stretches that watch over every departure and return.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Psalm 121:3-8 again. Notice what the keeper is doing while the traveler sleeps, and how long the keeping lasts.

comprehension_check.question: Psalm 130:4 says God's forgiveness leads to the fear of him. What is the psalm teaching about prayer from the depths?
options: Mercy is what makes approaching God possible at all
Guilt must be fully paid down before prayer resumes
Reverence requires keeping a safe distance until clean
Waiting wears down a reluctance in God to answer
comprehension_check.why: Psalm 130:4 locates forgiveness with the LORD himself, which is why the voice from the depths dares to keep speaking.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Psalm 130:1-6 again. Notice what the psalm says is with the LORD, and what kind of waiting that produces.

nodes.title: The Final Hallel: Let Everything Praise
nodes.summary: Five closing psalms that each begin and end with 'Hallelujah,' widening the choir from Israel to kings to sea creatures to 'everything that has breath.' The Psalter began with two ways and ends with one sound: praise.

prerequisites.reason: The final Hallel is Book V's — and the whole Psalter's — engineered crescendo.

connections.reason: Revelation's throne-room choruses are the final Hallel's vision realized: every creature praising.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Psalm 146 warns against trusting princes whose plans die with them, then the collection ends by calling everything that has breath to praise the LORD. What are you currently trusting that has an expiration date, and what would moving that trust toward praise look like?
assessment_questions: What word opens and closes each of Psalms 146 through 150, and who or what is summoned to praise by the end?

Psalm 146 warns against trusting princes and then lists what God does: justice for the oppressed, food for the hungry, sight for the blind. What do those actions reveal about why God alone deserves this praise?

Psalm 150 ends the whole Psalter by calling everything that has breath to praise the LORD. After all the laments and crises the book has walked through, what does it mean that praise gets the last word, and what would it take for praise to get the last word in your story?

teaching_concepts.explanation: These psalms ground worship in God's character and deeds, so praise is the truthful response to reality.
Psalm 146 contrasts mortal rulers whose plans perish with the God who keeps faith forever and defends the weak.
The God praised here feeds the hungry, frees prisoners, and upholds the fatherless and the widow, so worship and justice belong together.
Psalm 148 summons sun, sea creatures, kings, and children alike, and Psalm 150 crowns the Psalter with every breathing thing praising the LORD.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how the final Hallel closes the Psalter's journey from lament to praise, and name what Psalm 146 says about where to put your trust.

comprehension_check.question: The Psalter's last psalms warn against trusting princes even while calling everything to praise. What is that pairing teaching worship?
options: Songs about God should stay clear of political matters
Praise relocates hope from mortal power to God's faithfulness
Rulers deserve praise only when their plans succeed
Worship should petition whichever prince God has installed
comprehension_check.why: Psalm 146:3-4 measures every prince by his last breath, and the psalm goes on praising the God whose help outlasts him.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Psalm 146:3-9 again. Notice what happens to a prince's plans, and what the psalm lists God still doing.

comprehension_check.question: Psalms 148 to 150 widen the choir from Israel to kings to sea creatures to every breath. What is the crescendo teaching?
options: Praise belongs to worshipers whose laments were answered
Praise is Israel's assignment while the nations observe
Praise depends on using the instruments the psalm lists
Praise is what every creature's breath is for
comprehension_check.why: Psalm 150:6 ends the Psalter by summoning everything that breathes, all creation gathered into one closing word of praise.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Psalm 148:11-12 and Psalm 150:6 again. Notice who keeps getting added to the singers before the book ends.
